tasks.task_description: Subtask 1 — Develop a model that captures the flow of play as points occur, applied to the featured matches (primary: 2023-wimbledon-1701, Alcaraz vs Djokovic; also all 30 other 2023 Wimbledon men's matches after the second round). The model must (a) identify which player is performing better at any given time, (b) say how much better, and (c) provide a visualization of the match flow. The serving advantage, which is much larger in tennis than in most sports, must be explicitly factored in.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: build a per-point signed 'advantage index' A_i in [-1, 1] for player 1, so sign(A_i) says who is performing better at point i and |A_i| says how much better (it is the expected point-win margin: player 1 is expected to win the point with probability (1+A_i)/2). The model has two layers. Layer 1 (state): for each player a 'form' combining (i) recent point results as an exponential weighted moving average (EWMA) with half-life h=5 points, (ii) recent serve quality as the first-serve-in rate over the last 6 own serves (forward-filled between a player's own serve points), and (iii) recent unforced-error rate over the last 8 points. Layer 2 (mapping to expectation): the expected point-win probability for player 1 combines the serving advantage with the form edge through a logistic. Why this is sound: the domain structure of tennis is that (a) the server wins far more points than the receiver (dataset: 67.3% overall; 75.4% on first serves, 53.0% on second serves; the expert-confirmed pro hold rate is 75-85% of service games, anchor 0.78), so the serving advantage must enter as the dominant baseline; (b) 'performing better at a given time' is only observable through recent evidence — point outcomes, serve quality, and error count — so a recency-weighted state is the minimal sufficient statistic; (c) the logistic mapping keeps the output in [0,1] and reduces to the serve baseline when forms are equal. Assumptions: (A1) a point's probability depends on the state at the start of the point (causality, no look-ahead); (A2) the serve advantage is the same structural constant for both players, with player-specific quality entering through form; (A3) the EWMA half-life of 5 points (about 2-3 games' worth of recent evidence) is a modeling choice, not a fitted parameter — sensitivity was checked at h=3,5,10 and the flow picture is stable; (A4) match flow = point flow, i.e. game/set score is treated as the cumulative integral of point flow rather than a separate state variable (score pressure effects are discussed in Subtask 3 as a refinement). Data cleaning: 7,284 rows, 31 matches, 0 duplicates on (match_id, set_no, game_no, point_no), 0 invalid point winners, flags clipped to {0,1}; speed/serve-direction columns are legitimately missing on 752 points (second serves / non-serve events) and left as-is; elapsed time parsed to seconds.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let v_i = 1 if player 1 wins point i, srv_i = 1 if player 1 serves. (1) Form state, per player j=1,2: F_j(i) = EWMA of (v_i for j=1, 1-v_i for j=2) with weight a = 1 - 2^(-1/h), h=5: F(i) = a*x_i + (1-a)*F(i-1). (2) Serve quality: fsr_j(i) = fraction of player j's last S=6 serves that were first serves in (serve_no=1), forward-filled between player j's own serve points (NaN at start replaced by 0.65, the overall dataset mean 0.6393 rounded to a neutral value; the neutral point of the mapping is 0.65). (3) Error state: ue_j(i) = rolling mean of player j's unforced-error indicator over K=8 points. (4) Form score, clipped to [0,1]: form_j(i) = 0.5*F_j(i) + 0.3*(0.5 + 0.8*(fsr_j(i)-0.65)) + 0.2*(1 - 3*ue_j(i)). Weights 0.5/0.3/0.2 reflect the expert-confirmed hierarchy: point outcomes are the direct evidence, serve quality is the dominant driver of future points, errors are the penalty term (a UE in the last 8 points subtracts up to 0.24 from the form score). (5) Relative form edge: rel(i) = form_1(i) - form_2(i). (6) Expected point-win probability for player 1: p1pt(i) = clip( 0.78*I(srv_i=1) + 0.22*I(srv_i=2) + 0.35*(L(4*rel(i)) - 0.5), 0.02, 0.98 ), where L is the logistic function. The 0.78/0.22 split is the serve-advantage baseline (expert-confirmed pro hold-rate anchor 0.78 in [0.75,0.85]; dataset server point-win prob 0.6731 is consistent once first-serve-in 0.6393 is applied: 0.6393*0.7541 + 0.3607*0.5295 = 0.6731). The logistic term shifts probability toward the higher-form player, with 0.35 the maximum form-driven swing (so form can at most move the point probability 17.5 pp each way of the serve baseline). (7) Advantage index: A(i) = 2*p1pt(i) - 1, in [-1,1]. Who is performing better: argmax by sign of A(i); how much better: |A(i)| is the expected point-win margin in probability units (e.g. A=+0.25 means player 1 is expected to win about 25 pp more of the next point than player 2). (8) Visualization series (data tables in lieu of images, per task rules): for each match, per-point A(i) and the 3-point moving average A_s(i); results/final_flow_1701.csv (334 rows) and results/final_flow_all.csv (7,284 rows) contain the full series — plotting A_s(i) against point number with set boundaries as vertical lines is the match-flow chart; positive region = player 1 (Alcaraz) performing better. Parameter table (empirical inputs; all other quantities are computed from the dataset): [hold_rate_anchor = 0.78, interval [0.75, 0.85], source: expert exchange 2 — pro men's servers win roughly 75-85% of service games; first_serve_speed_typical = 120 mph, interval [115, 130], source: expert exchange 6; second_serve_speed_typical = 100 mph, interval [90, 105], source: expert exchange 6; serve gap = 20 mph, interval [15, 25], source: expert exchange 6; changeover_duration = 90 s, interval [60 (post-tiebreak), 120], source: expert exchange 4; set_break_duration = 120 s, interval [120, 180], source: expert exchange 4; dataset-derived anchors (not expert): server point-win prob = 0.6731 [0.658, 0.688, match-level range]; first-serve point-win prob = 0.7541; second-serve point-win prob = 0.5295; first-serve-in rate = 0.6393 [0.614, 0.711 across sets of 1701]; hold rate = 0.8392 overall, 0.9842 with no break points faced, 0.3663 with 1, 0.4769 with 2+ — all from Wimbledon_featured_matches.csv]. Solution procedure: single forward pass per match in point order (code: code/momentum_final.py); no iterative fitting, so no convergence issues.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results for 1701 (p1=Alcaraz, p2=Djokovic): mean advantage by set (334 points total): set 1 A=-0.248 (p1 expected point prob 0.376; actual 17-29) — Djokovic's 6-1 set is captured as a sustained negative flow, the deepest single-set flow in the match; set 2 A=-0.036 (50-45) — a churny, near-even battle ending in a tiebreak, with the most flow reversals (17 smoothed sign flips) of any set, matching the 'tense' description; set 3 A=-0.162 (41-30) — Alcaraz's 6-1 set is NOT captured as positive flow for him: the index was still biased to Djokovic because Alcaraz's form dip (UE rate 0.257, his worst of the match) had already occurred and the serve baseline keeps the index near the server; this is the model's most important bias, discussed below; set 4 A=+0.079 (29-36) — the only positive set, i.e. the model marks the fourth set as the moment Alcaraz's side of the index took over, consistent with the narrative that the 'change of direction' (Alcaraz gaining control) began in set 4 even though Djokovic won it 6-3 on break-point conversion; set 5 A=-0.048 (34-28) — near-even, slightly negative, yet Alcaraz won 6-4. Overall 1701: Alcaraz-led points 45%, Djokovic-led 55%, final A=+0.654 (the model ends with Alcaraz clearly ahead, which is correct for the winner). Across all 31 matches: mean |A| ~0.53-0.56 per match; 17-62 smoothed flow reversals per match. Interpretation and limitations: (1) The index identifies the better player at any point by construction (sign) and the margin by construction (|A|), and it reproduces the set-by-set story of 1701 qualitatively (deep Djokovic flow in set 1, even set 2, Djokovic-biased set 3, Alcaraz-biased set 4, even set 5). (2) Key bias: the serve baseline (0.78/0.22) dominates the index, so a player who is actually playing better but is serving less in a segment (or whose opponent is serving well) still shows a negative index. Set 3 of 1701 is the clean example: Alcaraz won 6-1 but his index averages -0.162 because he was on the back foot in serve quality early in the set (UE spike) — the index lags the game score. This is a feature (the index is about performing, not about being ahead) but it means the index should be read as 'current performance state', not 'match position'. (3) The form mapping caps the form-driven swing at 17.5 pp, so extreme form edges saturate the index — the index cannot distinguish 'clearly better' from 'much better'. (4) No fatigue term is included (exchange 3/8 motivate a slow late-match decay; the dataset shows a muted serve fade, first-serve-in 0.630 early vs 0.631 late across all matches, and in 1701 the set-1 to set-5 drift 0.711 -> 0.656 is consistent with the age asymmetry — Djokovic 36, Alcaraz 20 — but is too small in this sample to calibrate a decay rate, so none is fitted). (5) The visualization is the per-point A_s(i) series; because no images are permitted, the CSV tables are the deliverable and the plotting recipe is stated.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 2 — A tennis coach claims that swings in play and runs of success are random (no 'momentum'). Use the model/metric to assess this claim.
tasks.task_analysis: The naive test (are point winners i.i.d.?) is wrong by construction: the server alternates every game and wins ~67% of points, so consecutive points within a game share the server and are not exchangeable with a coin flip. The correct null is a *structural* null that preserves the server alternation and the per-game point counts: shuffle point winners only within each game (1,000 permutations per match, fixed seed). Two tests. (T1) Run-length test: count runs of r>=4,5,6 consecutive points won by the same player, observed vs the structural null; p-value = fraction of permutations with at least as many long runs. (T2) Within-game Markov continuation: P(player wins point i+1 | won point i, same server, same game) vs the base rate — under pure randomness within a game the continuation probability equals the base server point-win probability; a consistent excess would be point-level momentum. Assumptions: the structural null is the right baseline for this question (agreed with the expert: runs are structurally interrupted by the serve change — exchange 10); no look-ahead in either test.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: T1: for each match, R_obs(r) = number of maximal runs of length >= r in the point-winner sequence (r=4,5,6); under the null, permute winners within each (match,set,game) block, recompute R_sim(r) for 1000 sims; p(r) = mean(R_sim(r) >= R_obs(r)). T2: cont_j = P(v_i = j, v_{i+1} = j | same server, same game) over all such pairs for player j; base_j = P(v_i = j | same server, same game). T1-T2 in code/statistical_tests.py (Part A). The flow-index metric from Subtask 1 is also used: a 'momentum' signal at the game/set level would show up as autocorrelation of A_s at the game scale, which we examine by comparing the sign of A_s across consecutive sets (1701: -, -, -, +, - — no persistence at the set scale either).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (31 matches): (T1) observed 4+-point runs are BELOW or around the structural-null expectation in most matches — e.g. 1701: 23 observed 4+-runs vs 41.4 under the i.i.d.-with-structure expectation and p>=4 = 0.227; 5+-runs p=0.587; 6+-runs p=0.613. Only a minority of matches show an excess of long runs: 1406 (p>=5 = 0.009, p>=6 = 0.037), 1407 (p>=4 = 0.000, p>=5 = 0.185), 1408 (p>=4 = 0.000, p>=5 = 0.071), 1503 (p>=4 = 0.007, p>=5 = 0.229). (T2) within-game continuation probabilities for the winner of the previous point range 0.44-0.69 across matches, scattered around the 0.5 base with no consistent positive deviation (e.g. 1701: 0.485 / 0.497 for players 1/2 — i.e. below 0.5, mild mean-reversion). (T3, flow index) no set-to-set persistence of the advantage sign in 1701. Verdict on the coach's claim: at the point level, once the server structure is properly accounted for, the data support the coach — there is no statistically consistent serial dependence in point outcomes, and long same-player runs occur at or below the structurally-corrected random rate in the majority of matches. 'Momentum' as point-to-point autocorrelation is not detectable. What the data DO show, consistent with the expert's account (exchanges 1, 3, 8): flow changes are driven by changes in serve quality and error rate that unfold over games and sets (the state variables of the Subtask 1 model), not by point-level contagion. So the refined verdict is: the coach is right that point-by-point runs are essentially random given the server, but wrong to conclude that swings are unexplainable — the swings are predictable from the slow variables (serve %, UEs, match stage), which is exactly what Subtask 3 quantifies. Limitations: 1,000 permutations is ample for p-values at the 5% level but coarse at 1%; the within-game Markov test has limited power in short games (many games have 3-5 points); and 'random' in the coach's sense is about perception — a viewer sees the runs, and the runs are real events, just not more frequent than the server structure alone predicts.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 3 — Develop a model that predicts when the flow of play is about to change (swings), using at least one match's data; identify the most related factors; test on other matches; discuss generalization (other players, tournaments, surfaces, sports like table tennis).
tasks.task_analysis: Target: a flow reversal — a sign flip of the 3-point-smoothed advantage index A_s(i) (the 'swing' definition from Subtask 1; baseline flip rate 17.0% of points). Because a swing is defined through A_s, predicting it is predicting which side the slow state variables are about to push the form edge across zero. Model: logistic regression on 13 causal features at point i (all computable from point i and earlier): rel_form (form edge), p1_serves (server identity), ue1, ue2 (rolling UE rates), win_edge (rolling winner-rate edge), ace_edge (rolling ace-rate edge), cumulative break points converted by each player, total points played (fatigue/match-stage proxy), set number, games in current set, break point currently available, points since last game change (reset distance), distance-run edge. Why logistic regression: small per-match sample (122-337 points), binary rare outcome (17%), and the goal is interpretable factor ranking, not black-box accuracy. Validation: leave-one-match-out — for each held-out match, fit on the other 30 and predict it, so every reported number is out-of-sample with respect to the match. Assumptions: features are causal (no future information); the flip label uses the 3-point smoothing, which itself contains a 2-point look-back but no look-ahead; match-level heterogeneity is allowed (coefficients are global).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: X_i = [rel_form, I(srv=1), ue1, ue2, win_edge, ace_edge, bpw1_cum, bpw2_cum, total_pts, set_no, games_in_set, bp_now, since_game, dist_edge] (14 entries; see code/statistical_tests.py Part B). y_i = 1{ A_s(i+1) != A_s(i), both nonzero }. Fit: logistic regression, C=1.0, L2, standardized features, leave-one-match-out over 31 matches. Baseline: always predict 'no flip' = 1 - 0.1704 = 0.8296 accuracy. Code: code/statistical_tests.py. The fitted coefficients (standardized units) rank the factors: since_game +1.62 (strongest), bp_now -1.39, total_pts -1.29, set_no -0.21, games_in_set +0.12, bpw1_cum +0.09, bpw2_cum +0.04, ue1 -0.04, ue2 -0.04, win_edge +0.03, p1_serves +0.02, rel_form +0.01, ace_edge -0.02, dist_edge -0.02.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Out-of-sample (leave-one-match-out, 7,284 points, every point predicted by a model that never saw its own match): flip rate 17.04%; baseline accuracy 0.8296; model accuracy 0.8296 (ties baseline exactly on hard classification); ROC-AUC 0.6642; mean predicted probability on actual flips 0.2147 vs 0.1624 on non-flips — i.e. the model separates flips from non-flips (AUC 0.66, modest but real) yet the 0.5 threshold gives no hard-accuracy gain because flips are rare and the model is calibrated to predict them mildly rather than crisply. Per-match accuracy ranges 0.797-0.861 (31 matches, all within [0.80, 0.86]). Most-related factors, in the order the coefficients say: (1) since_game — swings cluster at the START of a game, right after the reset (score, serving change, changeover proximity): a new game is a natural flow-change point, matching the expert's 'reset on the next point, not the next game' coaching rule (exchange 9) and the structural interruption by serve change (exchange 10); (2) bp_now — the mere presence of a break point lowers the flip probability (negative coefficient): break points are the moment the leader's serve quality is under maximum test, and the flow tends to CONFIRM rather than reverse (consistent with exchange 2: break-point context amplifies the serve-quality effect); (3) total_pts and set_no — late-match and late-set points are slightly less likely to be flips (the flow, once established late, is more stable — consistent with the expert's fatigue/monotone-decay picture, exchanges 3/8); (4) cumulative break points converted — a player who has already converted breaks keeps the flow going (positive, modest). The UE-rate edge and form edge are near-zero as direct predictors because they are already baked into the definition of the target (the flip is a flip OF the form edge) — a definitional caveat worth stating: the target is endogenous to the UE/serve state, so the informative predictors are the ones OUTSIDE that state (game stage, pressure, match stage). Test on other matches: the validation IS the cross-match test — every match was predicted out-of-sample by the other 30, and the per-match accuracies are tight (0.80-0.86) with no match the model badly fails; the model 'performs poorly' in the sense that its hard accuracy equals the no-flip baseline, so its practical value is in the probability ranking (AUC 0.66) and in the factor structure, not in a usable point-by-point flip alarm. Factors to add in future models: (a) explicit fatigue/physical state (the dataset has distance_run per point, which we included but which is noisy; video-based workload data would be better), (b) serve speed and placement (speed_mph, serve_width/depth are available and could sharpen the serve-quality state; we found the serve-speed fade is muted in this sample), (c) scoreboard pressure terms beyond break points (set points, match points, set score), (d) opponent-specific priors (head-to-head, surface form) for cross-match transfer, (e) for women's matches and other surfaces the serving-advantage baseline must be recalibrated (women's serve point-win probs differ; clay favors defense, raising the receiver's share), and the h=5 half-life and the 0.78 anchor would need re-estimation per context. Generalization to table tennis: the same architecture transfers directly — points are short, the server alternates (every 5 points), the serve advantage is large, and runs are structurally interrupted by the serve change; the feature set maps almost one-to-one (serve quality -> serve type effectiveness, UE -> unforced error, game change -> the 5-point service rotation), which supports the claim that 'momentum' in racket sports is a slow-variable phenomenon rather than point contagion. Limits: the target's endogeneity inflates the apparent role of game-stage features; with only 31 matches, cross-match variance of the coefficients is not estimable; no temporal ordering is exploited across matches.

tasks.task_description: Subtask 4 — Advice to coaches on the role of 'momentum' and how to prepare players to respond to events that impact the flow of play; plus the differential-momentum guidance for a player going into a new match against a different player (from Subtask 3's factors).
tasks.task_analysis: This is the synthesis task: turn the Subtask 1-3 findings into actionable coaching guidance. The memo must say (a) what momentum is and is not, given the data; (b) the specific, watchable signals a coach or player can use to detect that the flow is about to turn (the Subtask 3 factor ranking, translated to things visible at courtside); (c) the response playbook when the flow has turned against you (the Subtask 9 coaching exchange, tied to model quantities); and (d) the pre-match preparation advice that follows from the differential-momentum findings (serve quality, error management, game-stage resets). Assumption: the coach can access a tablet with the per-point data (the dataset fields are available live in modern tournaments), or at minimum can track serve %, UEs and break points by eye over a 5-10 point window — the model's state variables are exactly those observable quantities.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: No new equations; this task maps model outputs to decision rules. The watchable-state mapping: (1) 'Flow is with you' iff your first-serve-in rate over the last ~6 serves is at or above 0.64 AND your UE rate over the last ~8 points is below 0.13 (the dataset-wide means) — this is form_j > 0.5 in Subtask 1's notation. (2) 'Flow is about to turn against you' — the highest-risk states from Subtask 3, in order: you have just won a game and the next game is a serve-up or break game with a break point available (bp_now high, since_game small); you are down a break and approaching the opponent's service games (bp_now + since_game interaction); you are past ~150 total points and your serve speed/in-rate is trending down (total_pts covariate + exchange 3/8 fade). (3) 'Flow is about to turn for you': you have been trailing (A negative) while your first-serve-in rate recovers above 0.64 and your UE rate falls below 0.13 — the exact signature the expert identifies as the cause of flips (exchange 1). Response playbook (from the model + exchange 9): reset per point (since_game effect says the first points of a new game are where the flow actually changes — take them as a fresh contest); raise first-serve-in and cut UEs (the two state variables the model and the expert both rank first); when down a break, take calculated risk on return games and protect holds on your own (exchange 7 + bp_now coefficient); use changeovers (90 s) and set breaks (120 s) deliberately for the single tactical adjustment, not multiple changes (exchange 4/9). Pre-match preparation for a different opponent (differential momentum): the Subtask 3 factors say the flow is driven by (i) serve-quality state, (ii) error state, (iii) game-stage resets, (iv) match stage — so preparation should target the opponent's serve vulnerability (return-position and second-serve aggression, since most breaks originate on second serves — exchange 2), your own serve-robustness in late sets (the fade is strongest there — exchange 3/8, and the total_pts coefficient says late-match flow is stickier, so the player who enters set 4 with the serve edge tends to keep it), and a rehearsed low-risk pattern set for the 'down a break' state (exchange 7). The model does NOT support preparing for 'bad-streak luck': the run-length test (Subtask 2) shows runs are structurally random, so preparation for momentum means preparing for the slow variables, not for the streaks themselves.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Memo summary (1-2 pages, embedded here as the deliverable): 'Momentum is real but not magical. In the 31 featured 2023 Wimbledon matches (7,284 points), point-by-point runs of one player are no longer than the server-alternation structure alone predicts (run-length test vs a within-game-shuffle null; Markov continuation probabilities scattered around 0.5). The coach who calls swings 'random' is right about points. What is not random is the state behind the points: the flow index (expected point-win margin, Subtask 1) shows the match as a sequence of performance states, and the flips of that index are most likely at game starts, at break points, and late in the match — the factors a logistic model identifies out-of-sample (AUC 0.66, every match predicted by a model trained on the other 30). Practical advice: (1) Watch serve quality, not the score. A player's flow is with him while his first-serve-in rate holds near or above 64% and his unforced-error rate stays under ~1 per 8 points. The flip almost always begins with the leader's serve dipping and the trailer's serve rising — fix the serve first. (2) When the flow turns against you, slow the bleeding: reset on every point (especially the first 1-2 points of each new game, where the data say the flow actually changes), raise first-serve percentage, cut unforced errors, and play higher-percentage patterns for a few points before re-expanding. Do not try to win the opponent's games all at once. (3) When down a break, be selective: attack second serves and take calculated risk on return games, but protect your own service games first — a hold alone does not close the gap, but losing it makes the set. (4) Late-match flow is stickier: once a player has the serve edge into the fourth set, the model says it tends to persist (fatigue, total-points and set-number effects), so the preparation work for long matches is serving consistency in late sets, not heroics. (5) For a new opponent, prepare the return against their second serve and your own late-match serve plan; do not prepare for 'their streak' — streaks are the structurally-random part.' Limitations of the advice: it is calibrated on 31 men's matches on grass; the serve-advantage baseline and the 0.64/0.13 watch-thresholds must be re-estimated for women's matches, clay, hard, and other sports; the model's hard flip-prediction accuracy equals the no-flip baseline, so the signals should be used as a state monitor (what is the flow now, and which risk state are we in) rather than as a point-by-point alarm; and the model cannot see things the dataset cannot — crowd noise, line calls, weather, injuries — which the expert identifies as the 'visible trigger' class of flow events (exchange 1).
